title: Idempotent Processing
description: Make your message consumers idempotent so that processing the same message multiple times does not cause duplicate side effects.

data.text: Idempotency means that applying the same operation multiple times has the same result as applying it once. In messaging, this is critical because most brokers offer at-least-once delivery. A message that was processed but not acknowledged before the consumer crashed will be redelivered. Without idempotency, the second delivery creates a duplicate side effect.

data.title: Scenarios that produce duplicates
items: Consumer crashes after processing but before acknowledging
Broker redelivers messages after a timeout
Application retries after a transient database failure
Operator manually re-queues messages for debugging

data.text: The simplest approach is to assign a unique identifier to each operation — typically the message ID combined with the entity being modified. Before executing the side effect, check whether this operation has already been applied. This pattern is the foundation of all other idempotency techniques.

data.title: Node.js — Idempotent payment processor
data.content: Store processed message IDs in Redis with a TTL to deduplicate.

data.text: When using a relational database, you can encode idempotency directly in the SQL. A conditional `INSERT` with a unique constraint, or an `UPDATE` with a `WHERE` clause checking the expected current state, ensures the database itself rejects duplicates without application-layer checks.

data.title: C# — Idempotent upsert with EF Core
data.content: Use a database-level unique constraint and catch the duplicate exception.

data.text: Strategy 3: Idempotency Keys in the Message

Many producers can generate an idempotency key before sending. The key is a deterministic hash of the operation parameters. If the consumer sees the same key twice, it knows the operation has already been attempted. This shifts responsibility to the producer but keeps the consumer stateless.

data.caption: Idempotent consumer flow using a processed message store
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    M[Message Received] --> K{Key in Store?}
    K -->|Yes| D[Return Success — Duplicate]
    K -->|No| P[Process Side Effect]
    P --> S[Store Key + Timestamp]
    S --> A[Ack Message]
    P -->|Failure| R[Retry / Nack]
    style D fill:#e8f5e9
    style A fill:#e1f5fe

data.title: Atomicity Matters
data.text: Store the processed key and apply the side effect in the same transaction where possible. If the store write succeeds but the side effect fails, you may block future legitimate attempts. Consider using a database transaction spanning both operations.

items.question: Should I use Redis or the database for deduplication?
items.answer: Redis is faster for high-throughput scenarios but is volatile. The database is slower but durable and transactional. A common pattern is to use Redis as a fast check and the database as the authoritative store.

items.question: What TTL should I use for processed message keys?
items.answer: Use a TTL that exceeds the maximum time a duplicate might appear. For most systems, 24 hours is a safe default. If your business requires reconciliation, use days or weeks instead.

items.question: Does idempotency guarantee exactly-once delivery?
items.answer: No. Idempotency makes at-least-once delivery safe, but it does not prevent duplicates from reaching the consumer. Exactly-once semantics require additional coordination at the broker or framework level.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Idempotency means multiple applications of the same operation produce the same result
Use unique operation keys stored in Redis or the database
Conditional database updates prevent duplicates at the persistence layer
Atomicity between side effect and key storage is critical
data.takeaway: Always build consumers as if they will receive duplicates. Idempotency is not optional — it is a reliability requirement.
